clean_text: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious , the Most Merciful. Praise be to Allah , and peace and blessings be upon the Messenger of Allah. To proceed, As it is in the book "Al-Wajiz fi Fiqh al-Sunnah wal-Kitab al-Aziz." The author says: "Then he would raise his back from bowing, saying," Meaning, while he says , During his saying: "Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah"(Allah hears those who praise Him). And "Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah." He would raise his hands during this standing position. Meaning, along with this standing position. And he says while standing: "Rabbana wa lakal-hamd." Sometimes he would add to that. Adding to that: "Rabbana wa lakal-hamd."" Rabbana lakal-hamd." "Allahumma Rabbana lakal-hamd." "Allahumma Rabbana wa lakal-hamd." These four are all narrated in the two Sahihs , so they are all authentic. As for "Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah," I say: "hamidah." However, when Arabs pause at a word, they omit the vowel on the final letter . So it becomes: "Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah," this. This only came in one form: "Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah." Then he says, "Rabbana wa lakal-hamd." "Rabbana lakal-hamd." "Allahumma Rabbana wa lakal-hamd." "Allahumma Rabbana lakal-hamd." Then he follows that with various types of supplications, and they are many. They have appeared in their designated sections in books of Adhkar ( remembrance). One can look them up and choose whatever one wishes from them. Sometimes he would add to that: " Rabbana wa lakal-hamd, hamdan kathiran tayyiban mubarakan fihi, mil'as-samawati wa mil'al-ardi, wa mil'a ma baynahuma, wa mil'a ma shi'ta min shay'in ba'd." For example, this is one of the supplications he used to say in this position. However, the mandatory part Is "Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah," which is during the rising. This is for the Imam and the follower. "Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah" is like " Allahu Akbar," the takbir of transition . "Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah." Then the mandatory part is "Rabbana lakal-hamd." This is the mandatory part , the minimum requirement. >> He says: "Then he would say takbir and descend into prostration, placing his hands on the ground before his knees." Some scholars say the opposite, that he places his knees before his hands. And this is the most correct view. And this is what the majority holds. The majority of scholars Hold that he places his knees before his hands. But there is no harm in this or that. If he places his hands before his knees , or his knees before his hands, there is no harm. But what is forbidden is to descend into prostration a camel. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, says: "None of you should kneel a camel kneels." Meaning, to drop down forcefully, descending from standing to prostration without composure. So if he can do it on his knees, it is more correct, and it is what the majority holds. If he can do it on his hands before his knees, there is no harm. But he should not descend a camel, descending without composure. This hadith, the saying of the Prophet ( PBUH) "None of you should kneel a camel kneels," does not mean descending on the knees or the hands, but rather the manner of descending. One should not descend, whether on his knees or his hands, unless he is composed. He says: "Then he would say takbir and descend into prostration, placing his hands on the ground before his knees, and he would rely on his palms, spreading them out, keeping his fingers together, and directing them towards the Qibla. He would place them level with his shoulders, and sometimes level with his ears, and fix his nose and forehead on the ground." And he used to say, "I have been commanded to prostrate on seven bones: the forehead," and he pointed with his hand to his nose. In prostration, I mean. And the hands, the knees, and the tips of the feet, and the tips of the feet. Not here, these are the tips of the toes . And not here, this is the back of the feet. And the tips of the feet; this position is the place one should prostrate upon. >> We ask Allah the Almighty to teach us what benefits us, to benefit us by what He has taught us, and to increase us in knowledge. And Allah knows best, and may peace and blessings be upon.

summary: Sh. Ali Mashhour provides a detailed fiqh analysis of the proper form and movements during the standing position after bowing (ruku') in Islamic prayer, based on Al-Wajiz fi Fiqh al-Sunnah wal-Kitab al-Aziz. He explains the prescribed supplications including 'Sami'a Allahu liman hamidah' and 'Rabbana wa lakal-hamd,' clarifying which portions are mandatory and which are recommended, with variations all authenticated in the Sahih collections. Sh. Ali Mashhour then addresses the proper technique for entering prostration, discussing the scholarly disagreement on whether hands or knees should touch the ground first, while emphasizing that descent should always be composed and dignified, never like a camel's descent. He concludes with the hadith regarding the seven bones upon which prostration should be performed: the forehead, nose, hands, knees, and tips of the toes.
